plain: Gemini is Google's artificial intelligence assistant. You write in English what you need and it answers, but you can also hand it a 300-page PDF, an hour-long video, or a whole spreadsheet and it'll answer questions about that. And if you ask for a website or a shop, it writes the instructions the computer needs to follow: you just copy, paste, and look. Think of a very fast intern who reads an entire tender document while you make coffee, and who also builds you the page while explaining it.

account.free: Yes, and the free tier gives you a lot. The gemini.google.com chat works with any Google account at no cost, with a daily cap on messages, uploads, and uses of the powerful model. The AI Studio key is also free and doesn't ask for a card: it gives you a few requests per minute and a few hundred per day, plenty for learning (exact numbers change every few months; they're at ai.google.dev/pricing). If you run short, the Google AI Pro plan runs around 20 dollars a month and Ultra around 250 dollars a month, and there's usually a free trial of the first one. Confirm the figure on the page before paying: prices and plan names shift.
steps: Sign in without registering for anything new

Go to aistudio.google.com and click 'Sign in', top right. There's no separate signup: it uses your regular Gmail account. If you have several, be careful which one you pick, because everything you do afterward is tied to that one.

The first time, a notice appears with two checkboxes: the terms of use and another one to receive emails from Google. Check the first one; the second is optional and you can leave it unchecked. Without the first, you can't move forward.
You'll see a big text box and, top right, a dropdown with the model's name. Type anything and click 'Run' or Ctrl + Enter. This just confirms the account works.

'Get API key' button, in the left column. It takes you to another screen with a blue button, 'Create API key'. It'll ask you to associate it with a project: if you don't have one, let it create one with whatever name it suggests.
Save it like you'd save a password

A string of nearly forty letters and numbers shows up, starting with AIza. Copy it and paste it into your password manager right then. You can look it up again from that screen, but don't send it over WhatsApp, don't paste it into a shared document, and don't show it in a screenshot.
Open the site where you'll actually work

For day-to-day use, don't use AI Studio: go to gemini.google.com. It's the polished version, with history, file uploads, the 'Canvas' button (it writes you the site and shows it running next to the chat), and 'Deep Research', which spends several minutes reading web pages and hands you back a report with links. AI Studio is the workshop; gemini.google.com is the car.
In gemini.google.com, bottom left, go into 'Activity'. There you turn off saving your conversations and choose how long they're kept. Do this before pasting anything from a client, not after.
account.warning: What you write on the free plan isn't private. On the AI Studio key's free tier, Google reserves the right to use your text to improve its models, and in the chat, with activity turned on, there are human reviewers who can read fragments; those fragments are kept for a long time and don't disappear just because you delete the conversation. In plain terms: no payroll data, no medical records, no client tax IDs, no internal company code, not until you're on a paid plan or have anonymized it. And a second warning: the day you turn on billing for that key, it stops being just a key and becomes your credit card. Whoever has it spends your money, and that spending can't be undone.

first: Go to gemini.google.com, click 'Canvas' below the text box, and type: 'a single-screen website for [your idea], with a contact form and a big button'. Within thirty seconds you have it working in the panel on the right, without installing anything.

Copy that code with the copy icon, open Notepad, paste it, and do File > Save As. Under 'Type' choose 'All files', name it index.html, and save it to the Desktop. Double-click: that's your first website, and you made it by talking.

Upload the biggest document you have on hand (a contract, a manual, this year's minutes) and ask it something specific that's only on page 200, asking it to copy the exact paragraph and the page number.
Upload a video of yours or paste a YouTube link and ask for a table of contents with timestamps in mm:ss format. Jump to one of those minutes and check it got it right.

Go to aistudio.google.com, click 'Get API key', and save the key in your password manager. Even if you don't use it today, the day you want Gemini working inside a spreadsheet or your website, you'll need it.
shortcuts: Ctrl + Enter (in AI Studio)
Runs the prompt without leaving the keyboard. You'll press this two hundred times a day. If it doesn't respond in your browser, the 'Run' button is right next to the box.
Enter and Shift + Enter (in gemini.google.com)
Enter sends. Shift + Enter breaks a line without sending. It's the difference between pasting one well-formed whole file and sending twenty messages cut off mid-sentence.
The '+' button next to the text box
Opens 'Upload files', the camera, and 'Add from Drive'. It's the door to everything good: PDF, images, video, audio, and your Google documents without downloading them first.
Typing @ inside the gemini.google.com box
Calls up other Google apps from the chat: @Gmail, @Google Drive, @YouTube, @Google Maps. With '@Google Drive find my March budget' it pulls it up without you leaving the conversation.
'Canvas' button
Opens a panel on the right where it writes the code AND shows it running. You ask for a change, you see it instantly. For vibecoding, this is where you'll live.
The model dropdown, up top
Switches between the fast model (Flash) and the powerful one (Pro). Change it based on the task, not habit: fast for writing and classifying, powerful for reasoning and hard code.
'Get code' button (AI Studio, top right)
Turns the conversation you just had into ready-to-paste code, in several languages. When something works in the chat, this button hands it to you as a finished program.
The edit pencil over your own message

Rewrites the instruction you got wrong instead of sending another one below it. Corrects course without dragging the mistake along: it's what separates a clean conversation from one that's lost the plot by message thirty.
The Gemini icon in the top-right corner of Google Docs, Gmail, Drive, and Sheets
Opens the side panel that sees the document in front of you. There you ask it to shorten a paragraph, draft the reply to that email, or summarize the file without opening it.
'System instructions', the collapsed box above the chat in AI Studio
Fixed instructions that apply to every message in that session without repeating them. This is where you paste your vibecoding rules so it never gives you code fragments again.
daily: Upload the whole document and ask specific questions, requesting the page and the literal paragraph. It can hold about 1,500 pages at once: chopping up the PDF is an old habit that now only hurts.
Vibecoding in a single file: always ask for the complete index.html, first line to last. You paste it into Notepad, save it as index.html, and double-click. No installing anything, no terminal.

When something breaks, paste three things together: the error message exactly as it shows, the whole file, and what clicks you made. With those three it fixes it on the first try; with just one, it guesses.
Video: upload the mp4 or paste the YouTube link and ask for timestamps in mm:ss. Useful for recorded meetings, classes, and picking apart what a competitor is doing without watching two hours of it.

Drive and Docs without downloading anything: the '+' > 'Add from Drive' in the chat, or the Gemini icon inside the document itself. No more downloading the file, uploading it, and downloading it again.
Create a Gem for whatever you repeat every morning (a text proofreader, an error translator, a quote drafter). You write the instructions once and stop repeating them.

Keep a project notebook in Google Docs and paste it in at the start of every new conversation. When the chat gets stuck, open a clean one and hand it the notebook: it's back up to speed in one message.

templates.name: System instructions for vibecoding
templates.what: The block of fixed rules that turns Gemini into a programmer who works the way you need: a single file, always complete, never asking you to install anything, and never giving you fragments you don't know where to paste. Works for any project that can be seen in a browser: a website, a simple shop, a calculator, an assistant.
templates.how: In AI Studio: open aistudio.google.com, click 'System instructions', the collapsed box above the chat, and paste this inside. It applies to every message in that session. gemini.google.com doesn't have that box: create a Gem ('Gems' in the left column > 'New Gem'), paste the text into the instructions field, name it, and save. From then on, go into that Gem and talk normally.
fill: [DESCRIBE IN ONE SENTENCE WHAT YOU'RE BUILDING]
Your idea told the way you'd tell your brother-in-law: 'a website where people book an appointment at my salon'
[WHO'S GOING TO USE IT AND FROM WHERE]
Customers on mobile, or you on a computer. Changes the whole design, so say it
[PASTE THE CURRENT FILE HERE]
The index.html that already works. If you're starting today, write 'nothing yet'
templates.code:
You're my programmer. I don't know how to code and I'm not going to learn.

PROJECT: [DESCRIBE IN ONE SENTENCE WHAT YOU'RE BUILDING]
FOR WHOM: [WHO'S GOING TO USE IT AND FROM WHERE: mobile, computer]
STATUS: [PASTE THE CURRENT FILE HERE, OR WRITE "nothing yet"]

NON-NEGOTIABLE RULES:

1. Everything in ONE SINGLE file called index.html: the HTML, the styles, and the JavaScript inside the same file. No installing programs. No terminal. No npm.

2. ALWAYS give me back the entire file, from the first line to the last, even if you only change one word. No fragments, no "replace line 40". I delete everything and paste yours.

3. Nothing downloaded from the internet (libraries, fonts, icons) unless I ask for it. If you think it's needed, ask me first and tell me why in one line.

4. Before the code: three lines at most saying what you changed and what I'll see on screen when I open it.

5. After the code: ONE single question, the most important decision you still need from me. Not two, not five.

6. Comment the code in English, one short line before each block, so I know where to make changes.

7. Plain, direct English, short sentences. No "Sure! I'd be happy to". No emojis.

8. If I ask for something impossible, very expensive, or that will break what already works, stop me BEFORE writing anything and offer the simple version that can be done today.

9. If something costs money, deletes data, or is irreversible, start your response with the word WARNING in capital letters and explain it in one sentence.

10. If you don't know something, say so. I'd rather hear "I don't know" than a nice-sounding fact that doesn't exist.

templates.name: Gemini inside Google Sheets with a formula
templates.what: A new function, =GEMINI(), that works like =SUM() except instead of adding numbers it classifies, summarizes, or translates whatever's in the cell next to it. Useful for processing 300 customer comments, sorting an expense list, or translating a catalog without copying and pasting 300 times.
templates.how: Open your spreadsheet. Menu Extensions > Apps Script. Another tab opens with an editor. Delete everything there and paste the code below. Change the key line to your own (from aistudio.google.com, starts with AIza). Click the save disk icon. Go back to the sheet and type in a cell: =GEMINI("classify this as COMPLAINT, PRAISE, or QUESTION", A2). The first time it takes a few seconds and may ask for permissions: accept them, it's your own script.
fill: PASTE_YOUR_KEY_STARTING_WITH_AIza
The key you got from AI Studio with 'Get API key'
gemini-2.5-flash
Leave it as is. The fast one is what you want for 300 rows; the powerful one would burn through your free quota
The instruction in quotes
What you want it to do, written as a command: 'summarize in 10 words', 'pull out only the amount in dollars'
A2
The cell with the source text. Then drag the formula down

templates.name: Gem 'Error Translator'
templates.what: A fixed helper you paste any red error message into and it always answers with the same structure: what it means, where it is, the whole fixed file, and how to check it. This is the one you'll use the most, because 60% of vibecoding is pasting errors.
templates.how: In gemini.google.com, left column, 'Gems' > 'New Gem'. Name it 'Error Translator'. Paste the text below into the instructions field. Save. From now on, when something breaks, go into that Gem, paste the error and the file, and that's it: you never repeat the rules again.
fill: Nothing required
This one's ready as is. If you always work on the same project, add a line at the end saying what it's about
The last line, the WARNING one
Keep it. It's what saves you from running something that deletes your work
templates.code:
You're my error translator. I don't know how to code and I'm not going to learn.

I'm going to paste you an error message exactly as it shows up on my screen, and often the whole file where it happens too.

ALWAYS answer with these four parts, with these exact titles, and nothing else:

1. WHAT IT'S TELLING YOU
A normal English sentence. If you use a technical word, translate it in parentheses the first time.

2. WHERE THE PROBLEM IS
The file and the line, if the error points to them. If it doesn't, write "the error doesn't give a line" instead of making one up.

3. FIX IT
If I pasted you the file, give it back to me ENTIRE and fixed, from the first line to the last, in a single block. If I didn't paste it, ask me for it. Don't guess what's in it.

4. HOW I KNOW IT'S FIXED
Exactly what I need to do (open what, click what) and what I should see on screen if it worked.

FORBIDDEN:
- Asking me to install programs, open a terminal, or "check the documentation". If there's genuinely no other way, say so in part 1 and explain why.
- Changing things unrelated to this error. If you see other things worth improving, note them at the end in a short list, but don't touch them.
- Saying "try it and see if it works" without telling me what to look at.

If the error could delete data or cost money, start with WARNING in capital letters.
Plain English, casual, short sentences.

templates.name: Project notebook in Google Docs
templates.what: A single document where your project's real status lives. You paste it in at the start of every new conversation and Gemini gets up to speed in one message. Solves vibecoding's number one problem: the 60-message conversation that's already contradicting itself and that you're afraid to give up.
templates.how: Create a new document in Google Docs and paste the outline below. Fill it in. Every time a version works, paste the whole file at the end, under 'CURRENT FILE', replacing the previous one. When the chat starts getting things wrong, open a new one and paste the whole notebook as the first message. Trick: instead of copy-pasting, in the chat click '+' > 'Add from Drive' and pick the document.
fill: [PROJECT NAME]
The real name, even if it's ugly. 'Salon bookings'
[Exact symptom]
The clicks you make, what you expect, and what happens. No interpreting: just what you see
[MAIN HEX CODE]
The color in #RRGGBB format. If you don't know it, ask Gemini to suggest three and pick one
[Paste the whole index.html here]
The last version that actually worked, not the one you're touching right now
templates.code:
NOTEBOOK FOR [PROJECT NAME]
Last updated: [DATE]

--- WHAT IT IS ---
[One sentence. What it does and for whom.]

--- WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE ---
[Describe the screen the way you'd describe it to someone over the phone. What's at the top, what's in the middle, what buttons.]

--- WHAT ALREADY WORKS ---
- [Thing 1]
- [Thing 2]

--- WHAT'S BROKEN ---
- [Exact symptom: what I do, what I expect, what actually happens]

--- DECISIONS NOT TO BE CHANGED ---
- Everything in a single index.html file
- Colors: [MAIN HEX CODE] and [SECONDARY]
- Text in English

--- NEXT, IN ORDER ---
1. [The smallest possible change]

3. [The next one]

--- CURRENT FILE ---
[Paste the whole index.html here every time a version works. This is your point of return.]

errors: API key not valid. Please pass a valid API key.

The key is copied wrong. Almost always a space at the start or end, or you copied only part of it. It starts with AIza and is nearly forty characters long. Go back to aistudio.google.com > 'Get API key', copy it in full with the copy icon (not by selecting with the mouse), and paste it again.
429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED - You exceeded your current quota

You've used up the free quota: either you went too fast in one minute, or you've exhausted the day's cap. Wait sixty seconds and try again. If it persists, switch to the fast model (Flash), which has a much wider quota. The daily counter resets on its own. Note: it's not a mistake in you or your code, so don't start changing things that were working.
503 UNAVAILABLE - The model is overloaded. Please try again later.

Google's servers are full, it's not your fault. Click 'Run' again in twenty seconds. If it persists, switch models in the dropdown: the fast one is usually free when the powerful one is saturated. Happens more during European afternoon hours.
User location is not supported for the API use without a billing account.

Google isn't giving out the free key from the country it's detecting. Almost always a VPN or proxy turned on: turn it off and reload the page. If you're in the US without a VPN and get this, try an incognito window with a clean Google session.
Request payload size exceeds the limit / 413 Payload Too Large

You fed it too large a file at once. Direct upload has a cap of around 20 MB. Fix: don't paste it inside the message, upload it with the '+' button or the paperclip. For video, upload it as a file in AI Studio instead of embedding it. If it's still huge, lower the video's quality before uploading.
The response comes back empty, or shows finishReason: SAFETY

The safety filter cut off the response. Tends to trigger with medical topics, legal topics, violence, or even aggressive marketing copy, and errs on the side of caution. Rephrase, asking for the same thing with different words and explaining what it's for ('for an internal report at my company'). If it's legitimate content of yours and it's still blocked, split it into smaller pieces.
#ERROR! in the cell, or 'Exception: Request failed for https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com returned code 400'

The Sheets script reached Google but sent it something wrong. Click the cell and hover to see the full message: it's almost always the key left unchanged (still says PASTE_YOUR_KEY) or the model's name misspelled. If the error mentions 'exceeded maximum execution time', the formula is taking over thirty seconds: ask for shorter answers with maxOutputTokens or drag the formula in batches of twenty rows.
The File is not in an ACTIVE state / 'Processing' that never finishes

You uploaded a large video or audio file and Google is still preparing it. Not an error, just patience: an hour-long video can take several minutes. Don't upload it again (you'll spend quota twice). If after ten minutes it's still the same, reload the page; if it disappears, upload it again at a lower resolution.

prompts.name: Have it interview you before writing a single line of code
prompts.prompt: I want to build [DESCRIBE IN ONE SENTENCE: a website, a shop, an app, an assistant] for [WHO'S GOING TO USE IT]. I don't know how to code and I don't plan to learn: you write the code and I copy, paste, and test it. Before writing a single line, interview me. Ask me up to eight questions, one at a time, waiting for my answer before moving to the next. Don't dump all eight at once. Only ask me what actually changes the outcome: what the person needs to see the moment they arrive, what action you want them to take, what happens right after they take it, what data needs to be stored and where, whether someone needs to log in with a password, and whether this needs to look good on mobile. Don't ask me about technologies, databases, or frameworks: you decide that and justify it to me in one line I can understand. If I ask for something impossible, very expensive, or that will take weeks, stop me and offer the simple version that can be working today. Once you finish the questions, write me half a page on what you're going to build and, below it, the list of what you're NOT going to include in this first version. Then wait for me to say 'go ahead'. Plain, direct English, short sentences, no emojis.

prompts.name: Ask for the first working version, in a single file
prompts.prompt: Go ahead. Write me the first working version of [PROJECT NAME], with these non-negotiable conditions. Everything in ONE SINGLE file called index.html: the HTML, the styles, and the JavaScript inside the same file, downloading nothing from the internet and requiring me to install no program or open any terminal. I want to be able to save that file on the Desktop, double-click it, and see it in the browser. Give me the entire file, from the first line to the last, in a single code block, even if it comes out very long. Don't give me loose pieces, don't tell me 'add this below that', and don't write ellipses to skip parts: I delete everything and paste yours. Add sample data so the screen looks full, not empty. Comment the code in English, one short line before each block, saying what that piece does, so I know where to make changes when I want to edit a text or a color. Make it look good on mobile. Before the code, tell me in three lines what I'll see when I open it. After the code, tell me the first thing I should test to know if it works and ask me ONE single question: the most important decision you still need from me. Here's the summary we agreed on: [PASTE THE SUMMARY FROM THE PREVIOUS STEP].

prompts.name: Fix something that broke, without it guessing
prompts.prompt: Something broke and I don't know why. I'm giving you everything I have so you don't have to guess anything. WHAT I DO, step by step: [DESCRIBE THE EXACT CLICKS, one per line]. WHAT I EXPECT TO HAPPEN: [WHAT YOU SHOULD SEE]. WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS: [WHAT YOU SEE, including if nothing happens]. MESSAGE ON SCREEN, COPIED EXACTLY: [PASTE THE WHOLE ERROR, without removing a single line even if it looks like illegible junk]. BROWSER AND SYSTEM: [Chrome, Edge, or Safari, and Windows or Mac]. COMPLETE FILE: [PASTE THE WHOLE index.html HERE]. Now answer me in this order. First, one plain English sentence saying what's happening, and if you use a technical word, translate it in parentheses. Second, point me to the culprit line and explain why it fails right there. Third, give me back the whole fixed file, from the first line to the last, in a single block. Fourth, tell me exactly what I need to do to confirm it's fixed and what I should see on screen if it worked. Don't change anything beyond what's strictly necessary to fix this: if you see other things worth improving, note them at the end in a short list, but don't touch them. If the error doesn't give you enough information, tell me what you need and how I get it, with the exact names of the menus I need to open.

prompts.name: Squeeze a huge document without it making anything up
prompts.prompt: I just uploaded [NUMBER] pages of [WHAT IT IS: a tender document, a contract, a manual, this year's minutes]. I don't want a summary: summaries of documents like this eat exactly what I need. I want answers I can verify in thirty seconds. Answer these specific questions, one by one: 1) [QUESTION 1]. 2) [QUESTION 2]. 3) [QUESTION 3]. For each answer, write three things, in this order. First, the short answer in one sentence. Second, the LITERAL paragraph from the document you're basing it on, in quotes, without changing a single word. Third, the page number and section that paragraph is in. If something doesn't appear in the document, write exactly DOES NOT APPEAR and don't fill it in with what's usually typical in these cases: I'd rather have a gap than a well-written invention. If two parts of the document contradict each other, tell me and quote both with their pages. If an answer depends on an appendix or refers to another clause, follow the thread and quote that one too. At the end, give me a list of the three things in this document that are going to give me trouble that I didn't ask about, each with its page. Plain English, no decoration or introductions.

prompts.name: Squeeze everything out of a long video without watching it again
prompts.prompt: I've given you a [DURATION] video that's [WHAT IT IS: a class, a recorded meeting, a product demo, a competitor's video]. I want to work with it without watching the whole thing again. Give me these five things, in this order and with these titles. 1) TABLE OF CONTENTS: timestamps in mm:ss format, one line per topic, with the topic title in four or five words. No more than three minutes in a row without a mark. 2) THE FIVE KEY SENTENCES: transcribed literally, in quotes, with their timestamp next to them. Pick the ones that change something, not filler. 3) WHAT SHOWS UP ON SCREEN: titles, slides, prices, web addresses, people's names, each with its timestamp; if something's hard to read, write 'illegible' instead of guessing. 4) DECISIONS AND COMMITMENTS: what gets decided, who says it if the voice is distinguishable, and by when. 5) WHAT'S PROMISED BUT NOT EXPLAINED: things mentioned in passing and left hanging, so I know what I'm missing. If any stretch has no voice and only shows something, describe what's shown. Don't make up timestamps: if you're not sure of the exact minute, give me the range. Plain English.

words: Prompt

The instruction you write it. The more specific, the better the result: 'summarize this' gives you mush; 'tell me what page discusses subcontracting and copy me the whole paragraph' gives you something useful.
Token
The little chunk the machine splits your text into to count it. A chunk is roughly three-quarters of a word. It matters because limits and pricing are measured in that, not pages.
Context window

How much material fits in a single conversation before it starts forgetting the beginning. Gemini's is a million of those chunks: about 1,500 pages of text in a row, or around an hour of video, at once.
API key
A very long password you give another program so it can talk to Gemini on your behalf. A person doesn't type it in: the program uses it on its own. If it leaks, others spend your quota or your money.
Model

The specific version of the brain answering you. Flash is fast and cheap, for summarizing, classifying, and answering emails. Pro is slow and expensive, for reasoning, checking numbers, or untangling hard code. The version numbers in front change every few months.
Multimodal
That it understands more than just text: photos, audio, video, and scanned documents. You show it a photo of the electrical panel and it tells you which breaker tripped.
Hallucination

When it makes up a fact with total confidence: a court ruling that doesn't exist, an article with a fake number, a round figure that sounds perfect. It doesn't warn you it's making it up. That's why numbers and sources always get double-checked.
Gem
A helper of yours with saved instructions. You configure it once ('always write in English, short sentences, no flourishes') and stop repeating that instruction in every new conversation.
System instructions

The fixed rules that apply to everything you discuss in that session, without repeating them in every message. In AI Studio they're in the 'System instructions' box, above the chat. This is where you put 'always give me back the whole file'.
Canvas
The panel that opens on the right in gemini.google.com and, besides writing the code, shows it running next to it. You ask for a change and see it instantly, without saving files or opening anything.
matters: Demand the complete file, always. Let it give you fragments ('replace this function with this other one') and you won't know where it goes, ending up with a Frankenstein file that won't run and that neither it nor you can fix anymore. The rule is sacred: first line to last, even if it's 400 lines to change one color. You delete everything and paste theirs.

The conversation gets poisoned. By message thirty or forty, with three failed versions mixed in, it starts blending old code with new and repeating mistakes you'd already fixed. Don't push through it. Open a new conversation, paste in your project notebook and the last working file, and continue. Saving the good version before every big change saves you whole afternoons.

The giant memory doesn't think for you. Upload the full 400 pages, sure, but ask specific questions and ask for the page. Whoever uploads a huge document and types 'summarize' gets generic mush and then goes around saying the tool doesn't work. It's the number one cause of disappointment.

Verify exactly what sounds best. Gemini nails the professional tone, and that's what makes its mistakes dangerous: a flawless report with a made-up figure in paragraph four, or elegant code that calls a function that doesn't exist. When it gives you a number, a date, or a source, check it. When it gives you code, test it before showing it to anyone.
ignore: The 'Temperature', 'Top-P', and 'Top-K' controls in AI Studio's right column. They regulate how much risk it takes when writing. The default values are well chosen, and the day you need to move them will be because a specific task is screaming for it.

The race of new models and their comparison tables. Every few weeks one comes out with a higher number. Learning to ask for things well transfers entirely to the next model; the tables expire in a month.

Vertex AI, the version of Gemini that lives inside Google Cloud. It's the same intelligence with enterprise billing, permissions, and auditing wrapped around it. It'll make complete sense the day you're deploying something to production for a company; while you're learning, it just adds extra screens.

questions.prompt: You receive a municipal tender document: 340 pages in a PDF. Before Friday you need to know two specific things: whether they allow subcontracting part of the service, and what warranty period they require. You upload it to Gemini.

options.text: You write both exact questions in the same message and ask it to copy the literal paragraph and page number for each answer.
options.why: You gave it the whole document, which it holds with room to spare, and also told it exactly which needle to find. The detail that changes everything is asking for the literal paragraph and the page: it turns an answer you'd have to take on faith into one you verify in thirty seconds by opening that page.

options.text: You first ask it 'give me a summary of the tender document' and then look for your two answers inside the summary.
options.why: It's what almost anyone would do and sounds reasonable: if the summary covers what matters, it'll be in there. It breaks down by pure arithmetic. Squeezing 340 pages into twenty lines forces you to throw out everything specific, and subcontracting is one paragraph among thousands. The summary will tell you 'contract execution conditions are regulated'. That gets you nowhere.

options.text: You split the PDF into 25-page chunks and feed them one by one so it doesn't get overloaded.
options.why: It was the right technique a few years ago, when these tools could only hold a few pages, and that's why a lot of people still drag it along. Here it's overkill: 340 pages takes up a fraction of what it can hold. And it actually hurts, because the warranty period is usually in an appendix that refers to a clause in the body of the document, and chopping it up loses exactly that connection.

questions.explain: The huge memory saves you from chopping up the document; it doesn't save you from formulating the question.

questions.prompt: You work at a small accounting firm. You want Gemini to sort and compare twenty payslips that have real people's names, ID numbers, and salaries on them. You're on the free account.

options.text: You replace names and ID numbers with 'Employee 1', 'Employee 2', and so on before uploading anything, and keep the table saying who's who on your own computer.
options.why: It's the only thing that protects you going forward and looking back: what never leaves your machine can't leak, can't train a model, and can't end up on a reviewer's screen. And you lose nothing, because for sorting and comparing salaries the names are just set dressing. The important nuance: the correspondence table stays on your computer, don't upload it later 'so it understands better'.

options.text: You upload it as is, get the result, and then delete the conversation and turn off history.
options.why: It seems like a decent patch because in almost everything digital, deleting undoes things. Not here. Turning off history and deleting the conversation affects what happens from that point on, it doesn't rewind what's already been sent: copies kept for review can still be around months later, and if a reviewer already read that fragment, there's no button that gets it back.

options.text: You use the free AI Studio key from a program instead of the chat, because going through a technical channel means the data no longer gets used.
options.why: Sounds logical: the more 'programmer-like' something looks, the more private it seems to be. It's exactly backwards. That key's free tier is precisely where Google reserves the right to use what you send to improve its models; the one that doesn't do that is the paid tier, card on file. You changed doors, not houses.

questions.explain: On the free plan you pay with what you write: anonymize before pasting, because afterward there's no going back.

questions.prompt: You're 40 messages into building your website with Gemini. You ask for a small change to a button's color and it hands you back a file where the contact form, which had been working fine for three days, no longer works.

options.text: You open a new conversation, paste in the whole last working file, and ask only for the color change on top of that.
options.why: The problem isn't the color change, it's that the conversation is dragging forty messages with three dead versions mixed in and can no longer tell which one is the good one. Starting clean with the good file in front of it wipes out all that clutter at once. It's the reflex that separates people who make progress from people who spend the afternoon fighting.

options.text: You tell it 'you broke the form, fix it' and keep going in the same conversation.
options.why: It's the natural thing to do and sometimes it works. But you're asking it to fix a bug while looking at the same pile of contradictory versions that caused it. Usually it fixes the form and breaks something else, and two rounds later you don't even know which version was the good one.

options.text: You copy just the form piece from the old version and paste it on top of the new file.
options.why: Sounds like a surgical fix and it's the classic trap. That piece may depend on names, styles, or functions that are called something else in the new file. You end up with a mixed-up file that won't run and that nobody can debug anymore, because neither you nor it knows where each line came from.

questions.explain: When the chat gets stuck, don't push through: open a new one and paste in the last working version.
